title: Learn a Local Craft
goal: Your kid learns a traditional craft from the hands of someone who still makes it: a weaver, a potter, a carver, or a grandparent who knits. They read a finished piece like a detective, learn the craft in a real lesson, work out what the maker's time is really worth, then make a piece on their own and tell its story.
need: Someone who makes a traditional craft by hand: a local maker, a workshop or market stall, or an elder in your family
Money to pay for the lesson or to buy a piece from the maker
The craft's own materials, which the maker usually provides
A notebook for the craft file

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: Most families treat a craft as a souvenir stop: a quick look, a photo, a purchase. Your job is to find a maker who will teach, pay them for their time, and stay quiet during the lesson so your kid asks the questions and the maker does the correcting.

plan.what: Find the craft and read a finished piece (Steps 1 and 2).
Count the real cost, then make a piece alone (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.a: Ask at a market stall, a cooperative or your host. Many makers will show a curious kid for a small fee at a quiet time. At home, ask the oldest people you know what they learned to make by hand.

troubleshoot.q: The lesson is in another language
troubleshoot.a: Hands teach better than words. Learn three words before you go: thread, again and thank you. Then let your kid copy the maker's hands.
Good. Ask the maker what their first piece looked like. Most will laugh and tell you.

lesson.text: A craft is knowledge held in someone's hands. The materials, the patterns and the hours of work all tell you about the place it comes from, and the fastest way to understand it is to try making it yourself.
lesson.before: 'It's just a bracelet. Why does it cost so much?'

model.line: Six colours, a pattern that repeats every few centimetres, cotton dyed by hand.
Half an hour to weave two centimetres, with the maker fixing every second row.
About four hours for one bracelet that sells for $8. That's $2 an hour, before the cotton.
'It's cheap for how long it takes.'

lesson.modelNote: Nothing about the bracelet changed. Two slow centimetres made by their own hands turned 'it costs too much' into $2 an hour, and a price that suddenly looked low.

steps.title: Find the craft
steps.why: Most places have something people still make by hand the old way. Finding it is the first piece of detective work.
steps.kid: Your kid finds out what people here make by hand, using the Find the craft card in the Craft Toolkit at the end of the guide: what's sold at the market, what locals wear or use, what a host says their grandparents made. They pick one craft to learn.
steps.you: Ask 'What do people here still make by hand?' rather than 'What should we buy?' At home, ask grandparents and older neighbours what they learned to make.
ask: What do you see made by hand everywhere here?
Which one would you most like to try?
steps.tip: Markets and cooperatives often know the makers. Ask who made a piece, and whether they teach.

levels.explore: Spot three handmade things at a market, and pick the one you'd like to make.
levels.develop: Find the local craft and three facts about it before the lesson.
levels.extend: Find out how long people here have made it, and what has changed since.

steps.title: Read a finished piece
steps.why: A finished piece is full of clues about how it was made, if you look slowly.
steps.kid: Your kid studies one finished piece up close, using the Read a piece card: what it's made of, the colours and pattern, the tools it needed and the marks of a hand. Then they guess how many hours it took.
steps.you: Ask the seller before anyone touches it. Write down your kid's hour guess; you'll check it after the lesson.
ask: What do you think it's made of?
How long do you think it took to make?
steps.tip: In some places a pattern or colour shows where a piece comes from or what it's for. Ask what this one means.

levels.explore: Look closely at one piece, and draw its pattern.
levels.develop: Fill in the Read a piece card, and guess the hours.
levels.extend: Compare a handmade piece with a machine-made copy, and list every difference you can find.

steps.title: Learn it from the maker
steps.why: Hands teach what no video can: the pressure, the rhythm, the small fixes.
steps.kid: Your kid takes a real lesson. They watch first, ask the questions on the Ask the maker card, then make a small piece with their own hands while the maker corrects them.
steps.you: Pay the maker for their time. Stand back and let the maker do the teaching. Handle sharp tools, hot kilns and dye pots yourself, and ask before taking photos.
ask: Who taught you, and how old were you?
What do beginners always get wrong?
steps.tip: Time how long your kid's small piece takes. You'll need that number in the next step.

levels.explore: Watch the maker, then do one part yourself with their help.
levels.develop: Make a small piece in the lesson, and ask two questions from the card.
levels.extend: Ask the maker what's hardest about earning a living from the craft, and write down the answer.

steps.title: Count the real cost
steps.why: Once you've tried it, the price of a handmade piece starts to make sense.
steps.kid: Your kid works out the real cost of one finished piece, using the Count the cost card: the hours, the materials and the price it sells for. They divide to find what the maker earns per hour, then compare it with a machine-made copy.
steps.you: Help with the division. Then ask the question that matters: 'Is that a fair price?' Let them decide what they'd charge.
ask: How close was your hour guess?
What would be a fair price, and why?
steps.tip: Use their own timing. If two centimetres took them 30 minutes, how long would the whole piece take them?

levels.explore: Count how long your small piece took, and say if the real price feels fair.
levels.develop: Work out what the maker earns per hour on one piece.
levels.extend: Find out how much of the shop price reaches the maker when a reseller sells it, and work out the maker's hourly pay that way.

steps.title: Make one on your own
steps.why: Making a second piece without help shows what really stuck.
steps.kid: Your kid makes a second piece on their own, using what they learned. Then they write its story on the Story card: who taught them, where the materials came from, what the pattern means and how long it took.
steps.you: Help them get the materials, then step away. If they want to use the maker's pattern, ask the maker first. When it's done, ask them to tell the story out loud to someone who wasn't there.
ask: What did you remember, and what did you have to work out?
Who will you show it to?
steps.tip: Keep the story with the piece. Ten years from now, the story is what will make it matter.

levels.explore: Make a small piece with a little help, and say who taught you.
levels.develop: Make a piece on your own, and fill in its Story card.
levels.extend: Change one thing, like the pattern or the colours, so the piece is yours, and explain what the maker would think.

conclusion.headline: They learned a craft from the hands that keep it alive.
conclusion.text: Pass a market stall with them a few weeks later. A kid who has made even one small piece by hand picks things up differently, turns them over, and asks who made them.
conclusion.celebrate: When they tell the story of their piece to someone, say: 'That piece has a teacher, a place and your own hours in it.'
extensions: Find the same craft in another place you visit, and compare the patterns, tools and prices
Learn the plant, animal or earth the main material comes from, and see it in the wild if you can
Price your own piece at the maker's hourly rate, and ask a family member whether they'd pay it.
Make a small piece as a thank-you gift for the maker or your host

signs: They ask who made something before they ask what it costs
They notice the difference between handmade and machine-made
They tell the story of their piece without being asked
makeItReal: This week, find one person who still makes something by hand, here or in your family, and ask if your kid can watch them work for half an hour.
